lesson.title: x to the x: When the Exponent Refuses to Sit Still
lesson.summary: Functions like x^x or x^(sin x) put a variable in both the base and the exponent at once, so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies on its own, and logarithmic differentiation becomes essential rather than optional.
lesson.body:
The power rule d/dx[x^n] = n x^(n-1) needs a constant exponent. The exponential rule d/dx[a^x] = a^x ln a needs a constant base. A function like y = x^x has a variable sitting in both spots at the same time, so it is not really a power function or an exponential function in the usual sense, and neither shortcut applies. This is precisely the gap logarithmic differentiation was built to close.

To differentiate y = x^x for x > 0, take logs first: ln y = x ln x. Differentiating the right side needs the ordinary product rule, since it is now a product of x and ln x: d/dx[x ln x] = 1 times ln x + x times (1/x) = ln x + 1. So y'/y = ln x + 1, and solving for y' gives y' = y(ln x + 1) = x^x (ln x + 1).

It is worth checking this two ways. At x = 1, y = 1^1 = 1, and the formula gives y' = 1 times (ln 1 + 1) = 1 times (0 + 1) = 1, so the curve has slope 1 there. Setting the bracket to zero, ln x + 1 = 0, gives ln x = -1, so x = e^(-1) = 1/e is exactly where the derivative vanishes, the critical point where x^x reaches its minimum. Both checks line up with the well known shape of the x^x curve, which dips to a minimum near x = 1/e and is already climbing again by x = 1.

For a genuinely mixed example, differentiate y = x^(sin x). Taking logs gives ln y = sin x times ln x. Differentiating the right side with the product rule gives d/dx[sin x times ln x] = cos x times ln x + sin x times (1/x), so y'/y = cos x ln x + (sin x)/x. Solving for y' gives y' = x^(sin x) [cos x ln x + (sin x)/x]. In general, for any y = f(x)^(g(x)) with f(x) > 0, the same three steps produce the master template y' = f(x)^(g(x)) [g'(x) ln f(x) + g(x) f'(x)/f(x)], worth remembering as the formula that covers every variable base, variable exponent function at once.
